  "core_problem": "Vision-language models answering chart questions cannot reliably map pixel positions to axis values — a deficit that persists even in the largest proprietary models. On ChartMuseum's visual reasoning tasks, Gemini-3.1-Pro achieves only 74.3% despite 95.1% on textual tasks (20.8pp gap); for open-source models ≤8B, the gap is far more severe. Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct — the current ≤10B frontier model — achieves only 27.8% visual vs 70.0% textual (42.2pp gap) against a human ceiling of 98.2% visual. Strikingly, this 42.2pp gap is larger in magnitude than the already-alarming proprietary gap, and it persists even when switching to the Thinking variant (Qwen3-VL-8B-Thinking: 32.4% visual, 76.4% textual — still a 44pp gap). Scale alone does not close this ratio gap, indicating the bottleneck is a missing training signal for calibrated spatial localization rather than general reasoning capacity. Specifically, models cannot reliably locate where on a chart image a given data value appears — a prerequisite for axis-to-value mapping, visual comparison, and line trajectory tracking.",
  "opportunity": "ChartMuseum (NeurIPS 2025) quantified the visual reasoning deficit precisely, and the May 2026 leaderboard confirms that this structural gap persists across model scale: even Gemini-3.1-Pro — the current SOTA at 80.7% overall — shows a 20.8pp visual-textual gap (74.3% visual, 95.1% textual) against a human ceiling of 98.2% visual. For the open-source ≤10B frontier, Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct (40.0% overall, 27.8% visual, 70.0% textual) shows a catastrophic 42.2pp visual-textual gap — larger in magnitude than the already-severe proprietary gap, and driven by a textual capability (70.0%) that general scaling has delivered while leaving visual localization behind. Qwen2.5-VL-7B and InternVL3-8B are no longer listed on the May 2026 leaderboard, having been superseded by Qwen3-VL models; Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct is the correct current ≤10B frontier baseline. No existing method addresses the root cause as a direct training signal: CogAlign (ACL Findings 2025, arXiv:2502.11492) trains perceptual invariance under visual transformations via DPO but targets 'is A > B?' reasoning, not 'at y-pixel P, what value is plotted?'; ChartPoint (ICCV 2025) adds bounding-box SFT anchors for region presence, not value-coordinate precision; RefChartQA (ICDAR 2025, arXiv:2503.23131) adds element-level bounding-box grounding via instruction tuning on 73K image-grounding pairs, improving ChartQA accuracy by >15% on element-localization tasks — but like ChartPoint, it supervises which chart element is present in a region, not what normalized axis-coordinate a queried value maps to; Chart-R1 (arXiv:2507.15509) applies two-stage Chain-of-Thought SFT + GRPO on Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct with accuracy and format rewards, achieving 34.8% overall on ChartMuseum without any coordinate supervision; BigCharts-R1 and Chart-RL use GRPO with answer-accuracy rewards only; ChartGen (2025) generates chart-to-code pairs for code reconstruction tasks, not coordinate calibration. Synthetic chart renderers (matplotlib/plotly) provide programmatic pixel↔value ground truth at zero marginal cost — an untapped training signal that enables calibrated axis localization supervision. The ChartQA training split (~28K real-world chart QA examples) provides a proven GRPO training corpus (validated by BigCharts-R1, COLM 2025) without any risk of benchmark contamination.",
  "landscape": "Current ChartMuseum leaderboard (May 2026): Gemini-3.1-Pro leads at 80.7% overall (74.3% visual, 95.1% textual), followed by Gemini-3-Flash at 78.6% (70.0% visual, 92.7% textual), GPT-5.2 at 77.0% (70.8% visual, 94.3% textual), and Gemma-4-31B-Instruct at 71.1% (64.1% visual, 88.6% textual). Human accuracy is 93.0% overall (98.2% visual). All top proprietary models show a persistent 20–24pp visual-textual gap. Open-source models ≤10B on the current leaderboard: Qwen3-VL-8B-Thinking at 44.4% overall (32.4% visual, 76.4% textual — 44pp gap); Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct at 40.0% overall (27.8% visual, 70.0% textual — 42.2pp gap); Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct at 37.7% overall (25.3% visual); Qwen3-VL-4B-Thinking at 36.1% overall (26.1% visual); Qwen3-VL-2B-Thinking at 30.1% overall (20.6% visual). Larger open-source models: Qwen3-VL-30B-A3B-Thinking at 49.7% (38.8% visual, 82.1% textual); Qwen3-VL-30B-A3B-Instruct at 40.2% (31.4% visual, 73.2% textual). Qwen2.5-VL-7B and InternVL3-8B are not listed on the May 2026 leaderboard, having been superseded by Qwen3-VL models. ChartMuseum has no public training split: it provides only a dev set (162 samples) and a test set (1,000 samples); both are reserved for evaluation only. The visual gap is thus a structural property of chart VLMs that scale moderates but does not eliminate — and that targeted coordinate supervision may address mechanistically. ACCT targets the open-source ≤10B frontier where compute-efficient solutions have the highest marginal value. CogAlign (ACL Findings 2025, Huang et al., Salesforce AI Research, arXiv:2502.11492) investigates a related but orthogonal mechanism: it trains VLMs to recognize quantities as invariant under visual transformations (DPO on synthetic image-transformation pairs), finding the decoder rather than encoder is the bottleneck for visual arithmetic. CogAlign improves CHOCOLATE by 4.6% and MATH-VISION by 2.9% with 60% less training data than SFT — a strong result for perceptual invariance, but not for calibrated spatial coordinate mapping. ChartPoint (ICCV 2025) introduces PointCoT with bounding-box SFT grounding (+5.04% on ChartBench) but measures region presence rather than coordinate precision: the model learns to confirm 'value X is near this chart region' (bounding-box overlap), not 'value X maps to normalized position 0.47 on the y-axis' — the latter being what ChartMuseum visual tasks directly test. RefChartQA (ICDAR 2025, arXiv:2503.23131) adds element-level bounding-box grounding to ChartQA via instruction tuning on 73K image-grounding pairs (single-element extraction, Program-of-Thought, and GPT-assisted labeling), improving TinyChart accuracy by +17.42% on human-posed ChartQA questions; like ChartPoint, it supervises chart-element localization rather than the axis-value coordinate mapping that ChartMuseum visual tasks require. Chart-R1 (arXiv:2507.15509) applies a two-stage strategy — Chain-of-Thought SFT on 228K samples followed by GRPO reinforcement fine-tuning on 30K samples — on Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct with accuracy and format rewards, achieving 34.8% overall on ChartMuseum without coordinate supervision. BigCharts-R1 (COLM 2025, arXiv:2508.09804) applies GRPO with answer-accuracy rewards on a diverse replotted real-chart dataset using ChartQA training split; it evaluates on ChartQA, CharXiv, and FQA/DVQA/PQA subsets but does not report ChartMuseum scores. Visionary-R1 (arXiv 2025) adds a caption reward. Chart-RL (arXiv 2026) uses verifiable GRPO rewards. ChartGen (arXiv:2507.19492, 2025) generates 222.5K chart-code pairs for chart-to-code reconstruction — a complementary pipeline for chart generation diversity, distinct from coordinate-calibration supervision. None of these methods supervise the axis-pixel-to-value calibration signal. Beyond Pixels (arXiv:2604.21134, April 2026) grounds chart queries via inference-time MCP tool calls against chart specifications — orthogonal to training-time coordinate supervision.",
  "approach": "We propose Axis-Coordinate Calibrated Training (ACCT), a two-stage pipeline that injects explicit pixel↔value supervision into a VLM using programmatic ground truth from synthetic chart renderers, then extends this signal to real charts via bootstrapped calibration. We use Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct as the backbone throughout both training stages (the Instruct variant, not Thinking, to make GRPO rollout compute predictable; see Stage 2 for justification). No 32B comparison is attempted; we stay within the 16-day/200 H100-hour constraint.\n\n**Stage 1 — Coordinate-Calibration LoRA SFT (Days 1–2, ~35–40 H100 hours, unattended overnight run):** We synthesize 50K charts using matplotlib/plotly (CPU, Day 1, ~6–8 hours), extracting programmatic pixel↔value transforms for every tick and data point. The Stage 1 LoRA training job is submitted as an unattended overnight run at the end of Day 1 and completes by Day 2 morning (~35–40 H100 hours on one or two H100s in parallel). Coordinate tasks are constructed in normalized form — e.g., 'at what normalized y-position [0.0–1.0] within the chart plot area does value 7.3 appear?' — to decouple supervision from Qwen3-VL's effective spatial resolution (14×14px patches at 448px input, yielding ~32 vertical bins). Normalization is defined relative to the chart plot area (excluding title/margin), which is available exactly from matplotlib's ax.get_position() in Stage 1 and approximated via RANSAC in Stage 2. Bins of width 0.07 (≈32px) span 2–4 typical tick intervals, providing sufficient discriminative resolution while staying within the model's localization granularity. We fine-tune Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct with LoRA (rank=64, α=128) on these tasks.\n\n**Day 2 Tick Detection Pilot (go/no-go gate for Stage 2 coordinate reward):** After reading Stage 1 results (Day 2 morning), we validate tick-label detection quality on 500 held-out ChartQA real charts using the following concrete pipeline: (i) Prompt Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct with the exact template: 'Identify all y-axis tick labels in this chart. For each visible numeric label along the left vertical axis, output one line in the format — tick_value: <number> | bbox: <|box_start|>(x_min,y_min),(x_max,y_max)<|box_end|> — using Qwen3-VL normalized coordinates (0–1000 scale). If no tick labels are visible, output NO_TICKS_FOUND.' (ii) Parse bounding boxes and numerical values; filter for plausible y-axis positions (x_min < 0.25 of image width). (iii) If ≥3 ticks are detected per chart, run RANSAC linear fit (tick_center_normalized_y → numerical value). (iv) Measure: (a) fraction of 500 charts with ≥3 reliable ticks detected, (b) RANSAC residual distribution (median, 90th percentile). Go/no-go criterion: if VLM grounding achieves ≥60% chart success rate with median RANSAC residual ≤0.06, proceed as designed. If success rate is 40–60%, switch to a dedicated OCR fallback (PaddleOCR-VL for text bounding boxes, then filter numerics by position). If success rate falls below 40% even with PaddleOCR, drop the coordinate reward component entirely from Stage 2 and run answer-reward-only GRPO; report this as an ablation finding rather than a system failure. The tick detection pilot runs in parallel with paper writing on Day 2 and results are reviewed in the Day 3 human gate before Stage 2 begins.\n\n**Stage 2 — GRPO with Composite Reward (Days 3–10, ~90 H100 hours, unattended run):** We apply GRPO on ChartQA training split (~28K examples: ~18.5K augmented + ~9.6K human-written; the same corpus used by BigCharts-R1 for chart RL) with a two-component reward. Stage 2 is submitted as an unattended run beginning Day 3 evening, completing by Day 10. ChartMuseum has no training split — its dev set (162 samples) and test set (1,000 samples) are held out entirely for evaluation. We optionally supplement with 1K samples from PlotQA/DVQA/FigureQA (following BigCharts-R1) for chart-type diversity.\n\n**Backbone and generation cap:** Stage 2 uses Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct (not the Thinking variant). The Thinking variant generates 2K–10K token chain-of-thought prefixes per rollout; at 8 rollouts per prompt × 28K prompts, this would require 400+ H100 hours — exceeding our budget. The Instruct variant with max_new_tokens=512 (covering the ACT prefix + answer in all observed cases during Stage 1) caps compute to ~90 H100 hours.\n\n(A) Answer accuracy reward: exact-match or relaxed numeric match (≤5% relative error) as in Chart-RL and BigCharts-R1. (B) Coordinate proximity reward on real charts via bootstrapped calibration (contingent on Day 2 pilot success): (i) detect tick-label bounding boxes using the validated approach from the Day 2 pilot (Qwen3-VL grounding or PaddleOCR fallback); (ii) OCR the numerical value in each detected box; (iii) fit a RANSAC robust linear model mapping detected tick-center normalized-y → numerical value within the chart plot area; (iv) invert to get approximate ground-truth normalized coordinates for queried values. The proximity reward is r = exp(−d²/(2σ²)) in normalized space, where σ is calibrated to 1.5× the median RANSAC residual measured in the Day 2 pilot. When fewer than 3 tick labels are reliably detected on a given chart, the coordinate component is dropped and only the answer reward is used for that example.\n\n**Axis-Calibration Tokens (ACTs):** Before any answer, the model is trained to output a structured prefix mapping N tick labels to their normalized positions (relative to the chart plot area): '<ACT> tick_1: value=0 → pos=0.00; tick_2: value=50 → pos=0.47; tick_3: value=100 → pos=1.00 </ACT>'. This forces an explicit spatial intermediate step verifiable against rendering ground truth in Stage 1 and against bootstrapped calibrations in Stage 2. ACTs are strictly more precise than ChartPoint's region-presence bounding boxes and orthogonal to Chart-RL's answer-only GRPO rewards.\n\n**Differentiation from CogAlign:** CogAlign trains invariance of perceptual properties via DPO on transformation pairs; its text-decoder bottleneck insight motivates a perceptual retraining approach. ACCT targets a complementary and distinct failure: the model cannot read off a specific quantity from a specific spatial position even when the chart is not transformed. The two approaches address complementary dimensions of visual arithmetic failures: CogAlign for perceptual invariance, ACCT for calibrated spatial localization.\n\n**Differentiation from Chart-R1:** Chart-R1 (arXiv:2507.15509) applies SFT+GRPO on Qwen2.5-VL-7B with accuracy and format rewards, achieving 34.8% overall on ChartMuseum. ACCT uses a stronger backbone (Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct, which already starts at 40.0% overall), adds Stage 1 coordinate-calibration SFT (absent from Chart-R1), and introduces the coordinate proximity reward in Stage 2 GRPO — directly targeting the axis-localization failure that Chart-R1, BigCharts-R1, and all existing methods leave unaddressed.\n\n**Expected improvement range:** We target a 10–20pp gain on ChartMuseum visual tasks (from the Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct baseline of 27.8% to 38–48% visual accuracy), with 15pp as our central estimate. Four reference points calibrate this range: (1) Scale alone cannot close the gap: Qwen3-VL-30B-A3B-Thinking achieves 38.8% visual using 4× more parameters and extended thinking — this suggests that targeted coordinate supervision may bring the visual accuracy of 8B Instruct models into the range currently achieved by 30B thinking models by directly addressing the localization deficit rather than increasing compute. (2) Chart-R1 reaches 34.8% overall on ChartMuseum (vs our 40.0% overall baseline) using a weaker backbone and no coordinate supervision; ACCT adds the missing signal on a stronger base, enabling gains beyond what accuracy-reward GRPO alone can provide. (3) The 42.2pp visual-textual gap is structural: dense synthetic-renderer supervision provides exact pixel↔value ground truth for the precise capability ChartMuseum visual tasks test — a training signal entirely absent from all prior work — enabling closure that accuracy-only rewards cannot achieve. (4) ChartPoint and RefChartQA confirm that spatial supervision for chart VLMs yields measurable gains — ChartPoint's PointCoT achieves +5.04% on ChartBench with bounding-box region-presence supervision, and RefChartQA achieves >15% improvement on ChartQA with element-level bounding-box grounding. ACCT's expected gains are 2–4× larger because the supervision signal directly addresses what ChartMuseum visual tasks measure: not 'which chart element is near pixel region R?' (the question bounding-box grounding answers) but 'at what normalized axis-coordinate does value V appear?' (the question that drives all axis-to-value mapping, visual comparison, and line trajectory tracking on ChartMuseum). Normalized coordinate prediction is strictly more informative than region-presence bounding boxes for the axis-localization failure mode, and ChartMuseum visual tasks are specifically designed to probe this precision — making the higher expected gain well-motivated rather than speculative. A 15pp visual gain (27.8% → 43.0%) would close approximately 35% of the structural visual-textual gap and place ACCT above all ≤10B models currently on the ChartMuseum leaderboard on the visual-reasoning dimension.",

Issues: ["MINOR — SpatialVLM (CVPR 2024) uncited: SpatialVLM (arXiv:2401.12168) establishes the direct precedent for training VLMs on synthetic spatial data with programmatic ground truth (2B VQA examples, metric 3D reasoning) — the general principle underlying ACCT Stage 1. ## Summary of Both Papers

### 1. SpatialVLM (arXiv:2401.12168)

**Core Method:**
SpatialVLM presents an automatic 3D spatial VQA data generation framework that operates on real-world photographs rather than synthetic data. It generates spatial reasoning tasks programmatically with ground truth, scaling to 2 billion question-answer examples across 10 million real-world images—creating "the first internet-scale 3D spatial reasoning dataset in metric space."

**Spatial Reasoning Tasks:**
The framework trains vision-language models on two categories:
- Qualitative spatial relationships (relative positioning between objects)
- Quantitative spatial measurements (distances, size differences)

**Key Results:**
- Significantly enhanced performance on spatial VQA benchmarks
- Enables novel downstream applications including chain-of-thought spatial reasoning and robotics applications through quantitative estimation capabilities

**Distinction from Chart Axis-Coordinate Calibration:**
SpatialVLM focuses on understanding real-world physical space in photographic images—measuring actual object distances and sizes in natural scenes. It does not address chart analysis, axis calibration, or graphical coordinate systems. The approach is fundamentally about spatial reasoning in photographs rather than interpreting visual data structures.

---

### 2. SimpleSeg (arXiv:2601.19228)

**Core Method:**
SimpleSeg reformulates image segmentation as a sequence generation task. Instead of producing pixel masks or bounding boxes, the model directly predicts sequences of points (textual coordinates) that delineate object boundaries entirely within the language model's native token-generation framework.

**Segmentation as Coordinate Sequence Generation:**
Rather than using specialized vision-specific components for segmentation, SimpleSeg leverages the standard MLLM (multimodal language model) architecture to generate coordinate sequences that trace object boundaries, keeping everything in the language space.

**Rewards/Supervision:**
The approach employs a two-stage pipeline:
1. Standard supervised fine-tuning (SF stage) for initial learning
2. Reinforcement learning using IoU (Intersection over Union) as the reward signal to refine point sequences and ensure they accurately match ground-truth contours

**Distinction from Chart Coordinate Prediction:**
SimpleSeg's key innovation is demonstrating that "precise spatial understanding can emerge from simple point prediction" without requiring auxiliary task-specific components. This contrasts with methods that need specialized architectural additions for spatial tasks. The method challenges the necessity of complex auxiliary components in vision-language models for achieving spatial precision.

---

**Key Difference Between the Papers:**
SpatialVLM focuses on enhancing VLMs' spatial reasoning capabilities in photographic scenes through quantitative and qualitative spatial understanding. SimpleSeg, on the other hand, targets a specific downstream task (segmentation) by reformulating it as coordinate sequence prediction within a language model, using RL refinement to improve boundary accuracy. They represent different approaches to spatial understanding: one as a pre-training objective, the other as a task-specific reformulation.
